title: Interview notes and a salary folder
scenario:
You lead operations at a recruitment agency with 300 consultants. Your scored use case is: after each interview, turn the consultant's notes into a candidate summary in the agency's standard template. About 1,800 summaries are written a month.

The agency already pays for a business AI workspace that can host shared agents. There are no software developers on staff. The exhibit shows the requirements and the IT notes.
exhibit:
Candidate summary: requirements and IT notes (made-up example data)

Inputs     Consultant's interview notes (shared drive, one folder
           per consultant)
Output     One-page summary in the agency template (Word)
Rules      Template and writing rules exist; owner: Head of Quality
Systems    No custom systems needed for phase 1
People     No developers; IT admin can set up workspace tools

IT note on the workspace agent draft:
  Drive connection set to ONE shared service account.
  That account can also read the HR folder (salaries, contracts).
  Plan: share the agent with all 300 consultants.

questions.prompt: For phase 1, which path fits best?

options.text: Set up a shared agent in the AI workspace the agency already pays for, using the template and rules.
options.explanation: Right. The steps are covered, no custom systems are needed and there are no developers. A ready-made option with low integration effort fits.

options.text: Hire developers to build an agent from scratch on a model API, to get the most control over every step.
options.explanation: The Claude docs call the direct API the path with the most control, and the OpenAI docs rate its integration effort high. Nothing in phase 1 needs that control yet.

options.text: Adopt a large agent framework first, so the agency is ready for any future AI project it may want.
options.explanation: Anthropic's post recommends the simplest solution and warns that frameworks can tempt teams to add complexity they don't need.

options.text: Wait until a vendor sells a product made only for recruitment agencies, then buy that one instead.
options.explanation: Waiting gives up about 1,800 summaries a month of value. The existing workspace already covers the mapped steps.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk in the IT note?

options.text: Sharing with 300 consultants is too many users at once, so the agent will slow down for everyone.
options.explanation: The note says nothing about speed. The issue is which files each user can reach through the agent.

options.text: Using Word as the output format means the summaries can't be read by the workspace agent.
options.explanation: The note raises no format problem. The concern is the shared account's access to the HR folder.

options.text: Every consultant could reach salaries and contracts in the HR folder through the shared account.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's cookbook says that with an agent-owned account, anyone the agent is shared with can access those resources. Use each user's own account, or an account limited to the notes folders.

options.text: The consultants' notes are stored in many folders, so the agent can only read one consultant's notes.
options.explanation: The folder layout is not the risk. The risk is that the shared account can also read files nobody should see.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 must write scores back into the agency's own applicant system. An engineer from a partner firm proposes a large agent framework. What should you ask first?

options.text: "Can the framework handle any task we might think of in the next five years, not only this one?"
options.explanation: That invites the extra complexity Anthropic's post warns about. Size the build to the task you have.

options.text: "Can you show me what prompts and calls the framework really makes, and why we need it here?"
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says frameworks can hide the underlying prompts and responses, and that wrong assumptions about what is under the hood are a common source of errors.

options.text: "Is this the most popular framework on the market, so that we follow what other companies do?"
options.explanation: Popularity doesn't tell you whether you need it, or whether your team understands what it does.

options.text: "Can we skip testing phase 2, since the framework was already tested by the people who built it?"
options.explanation: The framework's own tests don't cover your applicant system or your rules. Your test examples still matter.
